title: Artist & Animator
tagline: Make pictures that feel alive, and then make them move.

stars.name: Shape & Form
stars.pretest: How would you start drawing a complicated object, like a person or a car?
stars.lesson: Every complicated object is built from simple forms: spheres, cylinders, boxes, and cones. Start with big, simple shapes to get proportion and position right, then add detail. Imagine drawing through the form as if it were transparent, which helps you understand how it sits in space. For living things, begin with gesture, a quick line capturing the movement and energy. Get the big idea in seconds before worrying about detail.

quiz.q: Why break a complex subject into basic shapes?
quiz.why: Simple forms let you check structure and proportion before detail.
options: It makes proportion and structure easier to get right

quiz.q: What is gesture drawing for?
quiz.why: A fast gesture records the action line of a pose, which gives life to the final drawing.

quiz.q: What does it mean to draw through a form?
quiz.why: Seeing the hidden sides helps you understand the object's volume in space.
options: Sketch as if it were transparent, including the hidden parts

stars.name: Value & Light
stars.pretest: Squint at your favorite picture. What do you still see when the details blur?
stars.lesson: Value is how light or dark something is, separate from its color. Strong images are built on a simple value structure: light, middle, and dark shapes arranged on purpose. Squinting blurs detail so you see those big value shapes. Light creates form: lit side, shadow side, and a cast shadow on the ground. Keep one consistent light direction, and plan values with small thumbnail sketches before you start the final piece.

quiz.q: What is value in art?
quiz.why: Value is lightness or darkness, independent of hue.
options: How light or dark something is

quiz.q: What does squinting at a scene help you see?
quiz.why: Blurring the details leaves only the main light and dark masses.
options: The big value shapes without distracting detail

quiz.q: Why keep one consistent light direction?
quiz.why: Conflicting lights confuse the viewer about the shape and position of objects.
options: It is a rule with no reason
So the forms and shadows look believable

stars.name: Animation Principles
stars.pretest: A ball bounces. What small things make it feel heavy, bouncy, or alive?
stars.lesson: Animators learned that motion feels real when certain principles are used. Squash and stretch gives weight and flexibility. Anticipation is a small opposite motion before the main action, such as a crouch before a jump. Slow in and slow out means motion eases at the start and end of a movement. Follow-through lets parts keep moving after the body stops. Arcs make movement natural, and exaggeration makes it clear.

quiz.q: What is anticipation in animation?
quiz.why: A crouch before a jump tells the audience what is coming and sells the force.
options: A small opposite movement before the main action

quiz.q: What does slow in and slow out mean?
quiz.why: Real objects accelerate and decelerate, so adding more frames near the ends looks natural.
options: Movement eases at the start and end

quiz.q: What does squash and stretch convey?
quiz.why: A ball that squashes on impact feels soft and bouncy, a hard ball would not.

stars.name: Composition
stars.pretest: Where in a picture should the most important thing go: dead center, or somewhere else?
stars.lesson: Composition is how you arrange things so the eye goes where you want. Start with a clear focal point, using contrast in value, color, or detail. The rule of thirds divides the frame into a 3x3 grid, and placing key elements near the lines or crossings often feels more dynamic than dead center. Leading lines, like roads or arms, point toward the focus. Empty space, called negative space, gives the picture room to breathe.

quiz.q: What draws the eye to a focal point?
quiz.why: The eye is drawn to differences, so contrast marks the most important area.
options: Contrast in value, color, or detail
Making it identical to everything else

quiz.q: What are leading lines?
quiz.why: Roads, arms, and rivers can steer attention.
options: Lines that guide the viewer's eye toward the focus

quiz.q: What is the rule of thirds?
quiz.why: Off-center placement often feels more dynamic than dead center.
options: Placing key elements near the lines of a 3x3 grid

stars.name: Perspective
stars.pretest: Why do railroad tracks seem to meet in the distance?
stars.lesson: Perspective makes flat paper feel three-dimensional. The horizon line is always at your eye level. In one-point perspective, parallel lines that go away from you converge at a vanishing point on the horizon, like railroad tracks. Objects get smaller as they get farther away. If you look down on a scene your horizon is high, and if you look up from the ground your horizon is low, which changes the whole mood of the picture.

quiz.q: Where is the horizon line in a drawing?
quiz.why: The horizon line is wherever your eyes are, which is why standing or crouching changes it.
options: At the top of the page

quiz.q: What happens to parallel lines going away from you in one-point perspective?
quiz.why: Parallel lines appear to meet at the vanishing point on the horizon.
options: They converge at a vanishing point

quiz.q: What happens to objects as they get farther away?
quiz.why: Size diminishes with distance.

stars.name: Color Theory
stars.pretest: If you wanted a bright orange to really pop, what color would you put next to it?
stars.lesson: Color has three properties: hue (the color itself), saturation (its intensity), and value (its lightness). Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as blue and orange, and make each other pop. Warm colors tend to advance and cool colors recede. Beginners often use too many colors, so choose a limited palette. Check your work in grayscale: if the values read well, the picture works even if the colors change.

quiz.q: Which color is complementary to blue?
quiz.why: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel. Blue's opposite is orange.

quiz.q: Why check a picture in grayscale?
quiz.why: Strong value structure carries a picture even when colors change.
options: To see whether the values read clearly
To turn it into a photo

quiz.q: What does saturation mean?
quiz.why: High saturation is vivid, low saturation is grayish.
options: How large the color shape is
The intensity or purity of a color

stars.name: Timing & Frames
stars.pretest: A film shows 24 pictures a second. How many drawings would you need for a 2-second shot?
stars.lesson: Animation is a series of still images shown quickly. Film typically runs at 24 frames per second, and animating on twos means one drawing for every two frames, or 12 drawings a second. Timing is how many frames an action takes: fewer frames feel fast, more feel slow or heavy. Spacing is how far an object moves between frames. In a bouncing ball, the drawings bunch up near the top of the arc, where it slows, and spread out near the ground.

quiz.q: What is a standard frame rate for film?
quiz.why: 24 fps is the long-standing cinema standard.

quiz.q: What does animating on twos mean?
quiz.why: At 24 fps that means 12 unique drawings per second.
options: One drawing is held for two frames

quiz.q: In a bouncing ball, where are the drawings closest together?
quiz.why: The ball slows at the peak, so spacing is tight there, and wide as it speeds up near the ground.
options: Near the top of the arc, where it slows

stars.name: From Idea to Film
stars.pretest: Where would you start if you wanted to make a 30-second animated short?
stars.lesson: A short film moves through stages. Start with the story, then storyboards, rough drawings of each shot. Next, an animatic: boards timed to sound, which shows whether the story works while changes are still cheap. Then comes layout, key poses, inbetweens that fill the motion, clean-up and color, and compositing. Get feedback early, because changing a board costs minutes and changing finished animation costs weeks.

quiz.q: What is a storyboard?
quiz.why: Boards let you plan the shots before the expensive animation work.
options: Rough drawings that plan each shot

quiz.q: Why make an animatic before animating?
quiz.why: Changing boards takes minutes, while changing finished animation takes weeks.
options: Timing and story can be fixed cheaply

quiz.q: What are key poses?
quiz.why: Keys set the major poses, and inbetweens fill the motion between them.
options: The main drawings that define the important moments of a motion
